The following is an evidence-based inference, not an official Hackfest scorecard.

| Judge | Technical depth | Presentation/business | Social or operational impact | Security and risk | Most likely decisive question |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ayushi Parashar | Secondary | Primary | Secondary | Limited evidence | "What measurable process or financial outcome does this produce?" [comparative_judging_matrix[0]] [11] |
| Shivani Prasad | Primary for data/process quality | Secondary | Secondary through mentoring | Limited evidence | "Does it work reliably, and what did the team learn?" [comparative_judging_matrix[1]] [18] |
| Sarthak Padhi | Primary | Secondary | Secondary, especially health applications | Methodological reliability | "What data, baseline, metric, and error analysis support the claim?" [comparative_judging_matrix[2]] [12] |
| Anjana Tudu | Primary when technology affects safety | Secondary | Primary | Primary | "Can this protect real users without creating legal, privacy, or abuse risks?" [comparative_judging_matrix[3]] [13] |
| Lingaraj Sethi | Primary | Secondary | Secondary | Primary | "What is the threat model, control, test evidence, and residual risk?" [comparative_judging_matrix[4]] [8][comparative_judging_matrix[5]] [15] |
| Sonali Satpathy | Limited technical evidence | Primary | Primary | Limited evidence | "Who adopts this, why will it persist, and how will the team communicate value?" [comparative_judging_matrix[6]] [19] |

The strongest overall strategy would be a working prototype with documented architecture and testing for Sarthak and Lingaraj, safety and deployability for Anjana, quantified workflow or business value for Ayushi, quality and learning evidence for Shivani, and an adoption-oriented impact narrative for Sonali.
synthesis:
| Dimension | Research and security judges | Operations and impact judges | Core trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Sarthak tests validity; Lingaraj tests security controls; Anjana tests safety in real enforcement contexts. | Ayushi tests operational economics; Sonali tests adoption and impact; Shivani likely tests data quality and team learning. | Novelty versus proof that a solution is safe, useful, and maintainable. |
| Scope | Models, architecture, threats, evidence, digital forensics. | Workflows, beneficiaries, finance, mentoring, management, communication. | A technically elegant subsystem may still fail as a product. |
| Time horizon | Correctness and resilience under future misuse or scale. | Near-term implementation, adoption, process improvement, and sustainable value. | Short demo success versus durable deployment. |
| Evidence base | Publications, cyber investigations, audits, technical talks. [synthesis[0]] [12][synthesis[1]] [13][synthesis[2]] [15][synthesis[3]] [16] | Enterprise-finance work, data-quality leadership, mentoring, and directorship. [synthesis[4]] [11][synthesis[5]] [18][synthesis[6]] [10] | Objective technical evidence versus credible but partly inferred commercial and social signals. |

The non-obvious tension is that the panel is not simply "technical versus nontechnical." Anjana combines a CSE degree and Ericsson engineering with police operations; her likely standard is not raw sophistication but technology that survives contact with victims, evidence rules, and adversaries. [synthesis[7]] [9][synthesis[1]] [13] Lingaraj similarly connects technical depth to audit and operational controls rather than research novelty alone. [synthesis[8]] [8]

Sarthak and Lingaraj may diverge even when both demand depth. Sarthak's public record points toward model methodology, testing, and domain evidence, while Lingaraj's points toward attack surfaces, controls, incident response, and forensics. [synthesis[0]] [12][synthesis[2]] [15][synthesis[3]] [16] An AI project could satisfy Sarthak with a strong benchmark yet fail Lingaraj because it leaks data or lacks authorization controls.

Ayushi and Sonali create the opposite pressure: a secure, accurate prototype still needs an implementable workflow, quantified value, identifiable users, and a credible adoption narrative. [synthesis[4]] [11][synthesis[9]] [19] If the GSK Shivani match is correct, her public post adds a useful counterweight to credential bias: demonstrated problem-solving and learning can matter more than experience alone. [synthesis[5]] [18]

The best cross-panel submission would therefore show five layers in order: a concrete user problem; a working end-to-end prototype; measured technical performance; explicit security, privacy, and failure handling; and a concise adoption and impact case. That structure does not assume an unpublished rubric. It directly answers the strongest documented professional signal from every likely judge.
